A.explanation: Current $I$ starts at zero and increases with $V$ but with decreasing gradient because heating of the filament raises its resistance.

B.explanation: A straight line through the origin shows constant resistance $R = V/I$, which is ohmic behaviour and not shown by a heating filament.

C.explanation: A falling $I$ as $V$ rises would need negative behaviour, whereas increasing $V$ must drive a larger $I$ from zero.

D.explanation: An increasing gradient means $I/V$ is increasing so resistance is falling, which is the opposite of a metal filament heating up.

hints: Notice the axes are $I$ against $V$ starting at $V = 0$, so check what $I$ must be when $V = 0$ and whether $I$ should rise or fall as $V$ is raised.
Connect increasing $V$ to heating in the filament: power $P = IV$ raises temperature and the resistance of a metal increases with temperature.
Use $R = V/I$ as the inverse gradient on this $I$-$V$ plot, so ask whether the gradient $I/V$ should stay constant, increase or decrease as the lamp gets hotter.
walkthrough: Identify the start point: when $V = 0$ there is no driving p.d., so $I = 0$. The curve must pass through the origin, which rules out a curve starting at maximum $I$.
State the heating effect: as $V$ is raised, current flows and dissipates power $P = IV$ in the filament, so its temperature rises well above room temperature.
Recall the rule for a metal conductor: higher lattice vibration at higher temperature scatters electrons more, so resistance $R$ increases with temperature.
Apply this to the $I$-$V$ graph using $R = V/I$. For a given $V$, a larger $R$ gives a smaller $I$ than for an ohmic resistor, so the $I$ rise slows down.
Therefore the gradient $\Delta I / \Delta V$ decreases as $V$ increases, giving a curve that rises steeply at first then flattens. This is option A.
